Raging Cape Fires

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The fire that drew the community together

Summary:
The fire started last Sunday and lasted 5 days. It destroyed 5500 thousand hectors of land and wiped out several houses. It's also a story on how capetonians came together to support the heros of the story, thats the firefighters.

Further information:
We go behind the scenes and speak to those involved. For example, the residents who lost their homes, an injured fireman and the fire chief.

Press Release:


Cape fires
Powerful fires fuelled by extreme heat and strong winds have wreaked havoc across the Cape Peninsula. After days of fighting the flames, it was finally contained thanks to the tireless efforts of firefighters and volunteers. Carte Blanche hears the remarkable narratives of bravery and compassion that have emerged from the ashes of the devastating inferno.


Script:


This last week, the country looked on in fascinated horror as Cape Town’s iconic mountain and forests disappeared behind a wall of flames – in a reminder of just how little control we have over this most awe-inspiring of elements.

Robert Williams: We had 5 minutes to get out of the house and it just went “PHWAAAH” and a big hurricane of fire just came around us

Awe inspiring but also absolutely devastating.
It is Thursday evening, and there is more optimism at the control center set up at lakeside fire station and Exhausted heads of dept. and fire personal assemble, some of whom who have not slept for 30 hours attend another briefing.
Chief Fire Officer (Sound Up): The situation now currently is currently a little bit better than it was 5 hours ago. One thing that we got to watch for is that the South Easter is coming up.
What has helped keep up the spirits of the fire fighters has been has the incredible outpouring of support from the community, even from up country visitors like this couple from Kwazulu natal who arrived late in the evening bringing refreshments.
Samantha Marx: There is so many people from so many different places here and we thought we no different from Durban. We want to help out where we can.
Last Sunday morning the fire began on the mountain above muizenberg. Over the next four days it spread to across the southern peninsula. It was clear that more resource were needed to compliment the professional firefighters and the trained volunteers.
Linton Rensburg: We soon realized this was a huge fire. This was going to be a huge fire and we were requested to bring in an additional 500 resources both local and from the rest of the country to fight this fire.
Not many people know that the dept. of environmental affairs has trained up over 5000 unemployed South Africans to be veld and forest firefighters.
And they were drafted into action but were up against a fire fuelled by extreme weather conditions - gusting winds and temperatures reaching 42 degrees.
JP Smith: We’ve had a fire born from extremely strong wind that then flipped around from us, that then gave us the hottest day in the history of the city since the early 1900’s.
Firemen are trained to deal with gusty conditions, which can result in fires changing course. But they can often take residents by surprise.
Ian Shnetler: If I put myself in a residents shoes it must be terrifying, almost feel helpless that things going to happen and you going to see your house go up in flames…
Which became a tragic reality for some Tokai residents.
LINK: THE FIRE HAS CAUSED ABSOLUTE DEVASTATION IN ITS WAKE. ON MONDAY MORNING RESIDENTS IN THIS PART OF CAPE TOWN SAW FLAMES COMING OVER THE MOUNTAIN FROM THE IRECTION OF OU KAAPSE WEG. BY TUESDAY AFTERNOON THE FLAMES WERE WITHIN 200 METERS OF THEIR HOMES.
Robert Williams: We were just fighting the fire, no sleep for 2 days, we just, it’s just unimaginable.
Robert and his wife with the help of neighbors and friends tried to do their best.
LINK: AFTER TWO DAYS THE WILLIAMS FAMILY THOUGHT THEY HAD WON THE BATTLE AGAINST THE FIRE BUT ABOUT 12 HOURS LATER THEIR WORLD WAS TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.
Robert Williams: We didn’t stand a chance even though those cyclones with the fire wall coming through its like just coming through while the wind, just fire and it hit through everything, set everything alight, you can’t imagine.
Two days after the destruction the family returned with their young traumatized children. Robert who had built this house with his own hands over the last four years had not yet organized insurance cover.
His neighbor Gerard O’Brien lives next to the Williams. He and a friend his friend recoded the wall of fired just before they evacuated.
Gerard O’Brien: The flames itself, they were about 30 to 40 meters high and the intensity of the heat, you could feel if you were standing here you would feel the heat from the forest.
John: How scared were you?
Gerard O’Brien: You know you thinking about your family and everything else you not thinking about fear until you standing…when these tree’s went up I thought that’s it. That’s when a bit of fear started trickling in.
Miraculously for Gerard and his family, his house was spared, and fireballs leapt over this house and torched his neighbor’s home. He ran to help the elderly couple.
Gerard O’Brien: He said he can’t find his keys and I asked him where’s your wife and he said she’s in the house. We managed to get into the house, kicked the door down, found the wife in the bedroom, wrapped her in a duvet, carried her out of here. Put her in his car which he had found the key of and told him to get the hell out of here.
The couple’s home was completely gutted. Whilst we were filming we saw friends looking for the elderly couples beloved cats that had fled.
Besides the wild life that was wiped out, the fire damaged 13 properties, four of which were completely destroyed including the well-known Tintswala Lodge in Houtbay. Firefighter Frank Forbay was first on the scene. He had dreamt of being a firefighter since being a young boy.

Frank Forbay: I had to walk past he firestation every Saturday and I always stood in amazement watching the firemen washing their fire engines and cleaning their engines and often I would hear someone say “wat soek hier daai” and they would chase me away.
Whilst trying to save the lodge, he unfortunately had to take off his soaked fire protective gloves to change from one hose to another thicker house.
Frank Forbay: As I turned around I heard this swooshing sound and a ball flames came through the door close to where I was standing of hot gas and I knew that it was a LPG cylinder that had exploded inside there.
Suffering intense pain Frank leapt into a nearby Jacuzzi. He was rushed to hospital and treated for 2nh degree burns. Happily he was discharged on Friday and is recuperating at home.
Jean De Villiers (Up Sound): I would like to do my part as well and I heard Bryan Habana pledged R5000. I would like to match that.
That’s springbok captain Jean de Villiers involved in a radio thong set up by PRIMEDIA’s KFM and CAPE talk 567 to raise funds for volunteer wildlife fire services and other organizations. A remarkable feature this last week has been how Capetonians and the rest of the country have opened their hearts and purses
Collen Louw: But there were beautiful contributions from pensioners, to 9 year olds to 6 year olds to the mom down the street to the dad in his office. We got calls from across the country from people who wanted to make a difference.
And with the help of corporates the station surpassed their R250 000 goal.
Colleen Louw: And after 8 hours we raised over 3 Million Rand.
School children, families and businesses literally dropped off tons of refreshments and other goods at fire Stations to help keep the firefighters in good spirits
Angelica Munoz: Although I’m not from here I feel like we all part of it. If we don’t do it together we cannot keep feeling sorry for the mountains and the animals and the situation. We all have to do something.
LINK: THIS IS ONE THE PLACES WHERE DONATIONS ARE BEING COLLECTED. FROM HERE THEY ARE PACKED INTO BOXES, PACKED ONTO VEHICLES AND TAKEN OUT TO FIREFIGHTERS IN THE FIELD.
Needing those refreshments were firefighters at the cape point nature reserve. Thursday was all about containment, with firefighters putting out fires that re-ignited. But we head that there was a huge blaze in cape point and with the wind picking up, nearby villages were in danger.
LINK: AS EXPECTED THE WINDS HAVE STARTED GUSTING THIS AFTERNOON AND A MASSIVE FIRE IS RAGING HERE AT CAPE POINT WITH AS MANY AS 5 HELKCOPTERS TRYING TO DOUSE THE FLAMES.
These helicopter were crucial to help to douse this fire and it was apparent that without this aerial support the fire could have done far more damage here and in other parts of the southern peninsula.
Over 190 hours were spent in the air involving 11 helicopter and 6 fixed wing bombers. In total 5500 hectors of terrain was affected.
John: I believe that the city’s firefighting capabilities have changed over the past 5 or 6 years?
JP Smith: I honestly believe that if this had happened five years ago we would not have been able to rise to the occasion as well as we are now. We have significantly better resources than we were in 2005/2006 when the fires really crippled us. There are a lot more staff, better training, better equipment, 5 more fire stations, 293 Million Rands of budget spent on the fire department.
Hopefully the heroes of this fire, the dedicated firefighters will have got some rest this weekend. They do their jobs because they want to make a difference. Frank forbay who was recently decorated for 20 years service cant wait to get back.
Frank Forbay: Something that grew on me from the very first day. I think I’m a people’s person. I’m there to help people; I’m there to help the community. If there is a call for help Frank Forbay will be there.
There is a silver lining to this story.
Paddy Gordon: We would be quite happy with the ecological impact of the fire. It is the fynbos kingdom, it does need to burn and most of that area was about 15 years old and ready to burn.
That is cold comfort for the Williams family who literally now have to pick up the pieces.
Robert Williams: It’s difficult to cope under this situation. It’s a worst nightmare ever. That fire took everything, it was horrendous.
Paddy Gordon feels for the people who have lost their houses.
Paddy Gordon: And obviously our hearts go out to those people that have those losses but in general the fire is going to have a huge positive impact on the mountain, on the people that use the mountain and even the tourism industry. After this fire we are going to see flowers and vegetation renewed, refreshed. It’s going to be a very beautiful place to be in.
